moment.title: A store's checkout, Monday 9:38 am
lines: 09:38:02 – handshake failed: certificate verify failed (certificate expired)
09:38:04 – handshake failed: certificate verify failed (certificate expired)
09:39:11 – upstream charge aborted: TLS layer rejected before HTTP
09:39:40 – certificate verify failed — 4,214 occurrences this hour
moment.question: What went wrong, and what would you check first?

options.label: The site's TLS certificate expired — check the certificate's expiry and the renewal job
The payment provider is down — reach out to the bank
A Monday traffic spike — scale up the checkout tier
Someone shipped a bug on Friday — roll back the deploy

moment.why: The log names the exact failure at the TLS layer and repeats it for every request: the certificate expired. Latency was normal and requests fell to zero at once — nothing about load or a deploy. Checking expiry costs one command.

drills.takeaway: An expired certificate fails every request at once — and one safe check tells you in seconds.
drills.teaser: A Monday where every payment dies mid-handshake — and the log says exactly why.

moment.title: The monitoring config, reviewed after the incident
lines: # alerts.yaml — checkout service
- name: latency-high     rule: p95 > 800ms for 5m
- name: error-rate-high  rule: http_5xx > 1% for 5m
- name: requests-fell    rule: rate < 50% of daily min for 10m
# certificate checks: expires soon
# "the TLS exporter never got wired up — backlog ticket open"
moment.question: Which failure would this config never catch in time, and what would you add?

options.label: Certificate expiry — add an alert when a certificate is within N days of expiring
HTTP errors — the 5xx rule is missing a per-route break-out
Slow pages — latency alerts should trigger at p95 > 400ms
Nothing — this set would have caught the outage already

moment.why: The outage produced zero HTTP 5xx responses — connections died at the TLS handshake before HTTP. None of the three rules watch certificate state. An N-days-before-expiry alert is the classic fix: alert while you can still act calmly.

drills.takeaway: Alert on certificates before they expire — not on the traffic they take down after.
drills.teaser: An alert file that watched everything except the one thing that broke.

moment.title: Storage maintenance log, 09:37 am
lines: 09:37:12 – playbook 'expire-old-servers' started (scheduled)
09:37:41 – subsystem REMOVE ran: 'removing a set of expired server entries from the index'
09:37:44 – index health: storage-node pool below minimum healthy threshold
09:37:52 – warnings: allocation requests have no free server to place data on
moment.question: What went wrong here, and what would you check next?

options.label: The removal removed far more entries than intended — compare the intended input against the change record
Servers physically failed during maintenance — check hardware alerts
The REMOVE subsystem has a bug — page its owner team
Retries overwhelmed the pool — throttle client traffic

moment.why: All events collapse into ten seconds: REMOVE ran, then immediately the pool is below threshold. The subsystem did what it was told; the input told it to remove too much. Check the change record: intended vs actual removed — that's where the real incident's answer lived.

drills.takeaway: When a maintenance step and an outage share a timestamp, read that step's change record first.
drills.teaser: A maintenance log where one line removed far more than anyone meant to.

moment.title: Index pool utilization, minute by minute
moment.question: What does this chart actually tell you, and what is the fix?

options.label: The index's view collapsed, not the hardware — restore the index's recorded entries
27 nodes went offline — provision replacements now
Traffic multiplied 3x — add client-side backoff
The utilization metric is broken — ignore it and check latency

moment.why: The key line is the last one: actual nodes online are unchanged. Only the index's belief about the pool changed. 96% 'utilization' is an artifact of a shrunken denominator — restore the wrong entries and the numbers recover by themselves.

drills.takeaway: When a metric collapses, ask whether reality changed — or only the system's view of reality.
drills.teaser: A capacity chart where only the system’s belief about reality collapsed.

moment.title: Overnight evaluation, per-class accuracy
moment.question: One class collapsed overnight while the average held steady. What went wrong, and what would you check next?

options.label: Something in last night's training data targeted that class — inspect the new batch's sources and labels
Real-world photo content drifted — schedule a data drift audit
The benchmark broke — re-run with a fresh held-out set
The model deploy broke that head — roll back the model

moment.why: The model in production was deployed days before the drop — nothing at the serving edge changed. What did change overnight was the retrain: its batch is the only overnight input. A per-class collapse with a stable average is the signature of poisoned or mislabeled data, not of drift (which degrades many classes gradually).

drills.takeaway: A sudden per-class collapse with a stable average is a training-data story, not an infrastructure story.
drills.teaser: An evaluation chart where one class fell off a cliff overnight.

moment.title: Ingestion pipeline config, two days before the incident
lines: # training-sources.yaml
sources:
- id: curated-internal   review: human
- id: partner-feed        review: human
+ id: scraped-bulk-bucket review: pipeline-smoke   # added last week
gates:
- schema-shape: pass required
- row-limit: 2.5M/day
- label_quality: required-if-configured   # never configured
moment.question: The model degraded after the new source joined training. What gate was missing, and where does it belong?

options.label: A label-quality gate — sample and review labels from any new source before it can enter the training set
A stronger pipeline smoke test — check more rows for schema validity
A lower row limit — cap any single source at 100K rows a day
Nothing — just never add sources without a two-week soak on shadow mode

moment.why: The new bucket passed schema checks, which say nothing about whether labels are true. The config even has a label_quality hook that was never configured. Size caps and shadow mode are useful, but the precise missing control is: humans sample labels from a new source before it shapes a model.

drills.takeaway: Schema validation is not data validation — new data sources need a label-quality gate.
drills.teaser: A config that fed 2 million unreviewed images straight into training.

moment.title: Auth audit log, 14:22
lines: 14:22 – password reset approved by the phone-based reset desk for 2 internal accounts
14:31 – those accounts logged in from 2 new networks, SMS second factor accepted
14:33 – MFA push approval in under 4 seconds — user was on a live call at the time (per calendar)
14:34 – 'delegate posting access' granted from those sessions to 9 verified accounts
moment.question: Reading only this log: what is the most likely story, and what is the first safe move?

options.label: Staff were socially engineered over the phone — verify with them out-of-band and revoke the live sessions and grants
An API key leaked — rotate all platform keys and audit usage
Malware on a staff laptop — image the machine and hunt persistence
The staff members did it themselves — open an insider-threat case

moment.why: The 4-second MFA approval while the person was provably on a call is a textbook live-session relay — and resets approved by phone don't need malware or leaked keys. Insider is the least-evidence story: a calendar and a session trail say 'tricked', not 'traitor'. First move: out-of-band verify the humans, then cut the sessions and grants.

drills.takeaway: A too-fast MFA approval from someone verifiably elsewhere means the human is being played in real time.
drills.teaser: An auth log where a 4-second MFA approval gives the whole story away.

moment.title: Admin-tools audit trail, reviewed post-incident
lines: ERROR audit-integrity: delegate grant S-114 → target verified accounts, no linked support ticket
ERROR audit-integrity: 9 grants in 11 minutes, all from one staff session, all missing ticket linkage
WARN   admin-tools: support-level session reached 'delegate posting access' — role allows it
INFO   posting-api: all 143 requests this window authorized correctly per existing rules
moment.question: The audit trail shows grants with no tickets, and the API says everything was 'authorized correctly'. What does that reveal, and what is the fix?

options.label: The authorization rules themselves were too permissive — the fix is least-privilege on the tool and out-of-band ticket validation, not just revoking
The posting API has an auth bug — audit and patch its grant path
The audit tool is throwing false errors — fix the ticket-linkage check
Revoking the grants is the complete fix — the system worked as designed

moment.why: The API followed its rules perfectly — the rules allowed a support-level session to delegate posting access for high-profile accounts with no ticket, no second approval, nothing. 'Authorized correctly' means the policy, not the outcome, was right. Revocation cleans today's mess; least-privilege plus out-of-band verification prevents tomorrow's.

drills.takeaway: When abuse is 'authorized correctly', the vulnerability is the policy.
drills.teaser: A trail of account grants with no tickets behind them.

moment.title: Trading engine order log, 09:34
lines: 09:34:11 – parent order 8F-22 re-sent; identical size, identical symbol
09:34:12 – child orders burst (n=214); fills genuinely flowing
09:34:14 – log field 'position-complete': never set
09:34:15 – code path id: routine 'PP-2003-test' — nobody on the bridge recognizes it
moment.question: What pattern is this log showing, and what would you check next?

options.label: Dormant test code is awake and its exit condition never fires — check last night's deployment record for flag reuse
The market feed is stuck repeating ticks — check feed timestamps first
A new strategy shipped a loop bug — roll back the strategy module
A client is algo-bombing through us — throttle their account

moment.why: Three tells: the same parent endlessly re-sent, 'never set' on the completion flag, and a code path nobody recognizes. That is old code running with a broken exit — feed problems look like stale data, not identical bursts. The deployment record answers whether a flag repurpose (a routine prep change) woke it up.

drills.takeaway: An exit condition that never fires turns old test code into an infinite, expensive loop.
drills.teaser: Order logs where the same parent sends forever and never completes.

moment.title: Overnight deployment record
lines: deploy purpose: enable tomorrow's new order type (prep only, no algorithm change)
mechanism: reuse existing feature-flag id rather than define a new one
flag id: defined 2018 for a retired test routine; code never removed
deploy status: rolled to 7 of 8 replicas (host 8 not included in the batch)
moment.question: Two landmines hide in this record. Which pair does the postmortem pin?

options.label: Reusing an old flag id (waking removed code) and a partially-applied deployment (7 of 8)
Deploying during market hours and a choppy market with the feed lagged
No autoscaling on replicas and risk limits too tight for burst flow
No code review on the flag change and no alert for unusual order rate

moment.why: The record says the quiet part twice: an existing id was reused, which is what woke the dead routine; and one of eight replicas was excluded from the batch, which is what turns any rollback into a partial one. The other observations are real-but-secondary — none of them causes an endless order loop.

drills.takeaway: Reused identifiers and partial deploys are the classic pair: old code wakes up, only most of the fleet agrees.
drills.teaser: A deploy record that reached seven servers out of eight.
